explanations.answer: They did evil in His sight
explanations.explanation: Judges 6:1 says, “Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD.” Look at that word “Again.” This wasn't their first time down this road. So He delivered them into the hand of Midian for seven years, and that's a long stretch, friend.

explanations.answer: They asked Him for a king
explanations.explanation: No king comes up anywhere in this verse. It says they did evil in the sight of the LORD, so He delivered them into the hand of Midian for seven years (Judges 6:1). Nobody here is shopping for a crown. Go back to the reason the verse actually gives.

explanations.answer: They left the land of Canaan
explanations.explanation: The verse never says they left anything. It says they did evil in the sight of the LORD, and that's why He delivered them into Midian's hand (Judges 6:1). In fact, Midian is the one who comes into the land to ravage it (Judges 6:5). Israel is hiding in it, not walking out of it.

explanations.answer: Up in the mountains and caves
explanations.explanation: Judges 6:2 says they prepared shelters “in the mountains, caves, and strongholds.” A whole nation moving into the hills to stay out of sight. I've slept in a junk drawer, so I know a bad bed when I hear one, and caves don't sound like a step up.

Jericho was a walled city, but this verse isn't talking about it. The text puts their shelters in the mountains, caves and strongholds (Judges 6:2). They're not behind city walls here. They're up in the hills, hiding.

The text sends them the other direction, friend. They don't go down to the riverbank. They go up, into the mountains, caves and strongholds (Judges 6:2). When you're hiding from an invader, you head for the high places.
That's the word. Judges 6:4 says they were “destroying the produce of the land.” Israel plants, and the invaders come up and wreck it. All that planting, and it never made it to the table.
Nobody's handing over money in this verse. The invaders aren't customers, they're wreckers. Judges 6:4 says they were “destroying the produce of the land.” Not a receipt in sight.

Counting is a good guess, but the verse has something harder in mind. It says they were “destroying the produce of the land” (Judges 6:4). And counting wouldn't have gone far anyway, since the next verse says the Midianites and their camels were innumerable (Judges 6:5).
Judges 6:5 says they came “like a great swarm of locusts.” Think of a cloud of hungry bugs landing on a field, except this cloud has tents and camels. That's the picture the Bible paints.
Water is a fair guess for something that pours in, but the Bible doesn't use it here. Judges 6:5 says they came “like a great swarm of locusts.” This invasion buzzes more than it splashes.
Lions would be scary, no doubt. But there are no lions in this verse. Judges 6:5 says the Midianites came with their livestock and their tents “like a great swarm of locusts.”
It's the other way around. Judges 6:5 says, “They and their camels were innumerable.” Innumerable means too many to count. Nobody was getting a clean headcount on this crowd.

Right, they couldn't be counted. Judges 6:5 says, “They and their camels were innumerable,” and they “entered the land to ravage it.” Imagine trying to count that crowd. You'd lose your place before you got started.
Judges 6:8 says, “He sent them a prophet.” A prophet is someone who speaks for God, so this man comes carrying the LORD's own message. Israel cried out, and the LORD answered with words for them.

No king shows up in this part of the story. Judges 6:8 says, “He sent them a prophet, who told them, ‘This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says…’” The messenger is a prophet, and the message is the LORD's.
A priest is a good guess, since priests had their own work for God. But this verse names someone else. Judges 6:8 says, “He sent them a prophet,” and he speaks what the LORD says.

explanations.answer: Not to fear the gods of the Amorites
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, “I am the LORD your God. You must not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell” (Judges 6:10). The Amorites were people who lived in the land. It's a plain reminder of who Israel's God is.

explanations.answer: Not to make peace with the Midianites
explanations.explanation: Peace with Midian never comes up in the prophet's message. What the LORD reminds them of is this: “You must not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell” (Judges 6:10). Stay with the words the verse gives.

explanations.answer: Not to plant their crops near Gaza
explanations.explanation: Gaza shows up earlier, as how far the invaders reached (Judges 6:4), but not in this reminder. The LORD says, “I am the LORD your God. You must not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell” (Judges 6:10).

The message says the opposite, friend. The LORD ends it with “But you did not obey Me” (Judges 6:10). That's a hard line to hear. But He started the whole message by reminding them what He had done for them.
Right. The message ends with the LORD saying, “But you did not obey Me” (Judges 6:10). It follows a list of what He had done for them. Hard words, but the prophet says them straight.

Judges 6:11 says Gideon, Joash's son, was “threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites.” I think a winepress is a strange place to thresh wheat, but I'd guess that's the idea. You hide your wheat where nobody's looking.

Caves were where the Israelites made shelters (Judges 6:2), so I see the thinking. But for Gideon, the verse says he was “threshing wheat in a winepress” (Judges 6:11). Same hiding game, different hiding spot.

His house is a sensible guess, but the verse puts him somewhere else. Judges 6:11 says he was “threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites.” Gideon's workspace is a winepress, no house in the picture.

The angel says, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor” (Judges 6:12). And remember where Gideon is standing when he hears it: in a winepress, hiding wheat. That's quite a greeting for that spot.
Joash is Gideon's father (Judges 6:11), so I see why that came to mind. But it's not what the angel calls him. The angel says, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor” (Judges 6:12).
That title doesn't appear in this verse. The angel of the LORD says to Gideon, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor” (Judges 6:12). Go with the words the angel actually uses.

explanations.answer: Then why has all this happened to us
explanations.explanation: Gideon says, “if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us?” (Judges 6:13). He doesn't tiptoe around it. He opens with “Please, my Lord,” and then he asks the hard question out loud.

explanations.answer: Then why hasn't He sent us a king
explanations.explanation: A king never comes up in Gideon's question. He asks, “if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us?” (Judges 6:13). He's asking about what Israel has gone through, not about a throne.

explanations.answer: Then why is our harvest so small
explanations.explanation: The harvest is a real problem in this story, but Gideon asks bigger than that. He says, “if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us?” (Judges 6:13). It's about all of it, not just the crops.
He does. Gideon says, “But now the LORD has forsaken us and delivered us into the hand of Midian” (Judges 6:13). Those are his words, said out loud to the angel. He holds nothing back, friend.

It's true, because Gideon says it right there. After asking about the wonders his fathers told him about, he says, “But now the LORD has forsaken us and delivered us into the hand of Midian” (Judges 6:13). Those are Gideon's words, and he says them plain.

The LORD says, “Go in the strength you have and save Israel from the hand of Midian” (Judges 6:14). That's the job, and it lands on the man who was hiding wheat in a winepress. Gideon sure didn't see that coming.

Going back to Egypt is not the plan at all. The LORD had already brought them up out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery (Judges 6:8). Now He tells Gideon, “save Israel from the hand of Midian” (Judges 6:14).

Guarding wheat is a small job next to this one. The LORD says, “Go in the strength you have and save Israel from the hand of Midian” (Judges 6:14). He's talking about the whole nation, not one pile of grain.

Gideon says, “my clan is the weakest in Manasseh” (Judges 6:15). Manasseh was one of Israel's tribes. He lists his weak spots like he's reading a résumé nobody should hire. And I'm in no position to laugh, I got hired out of a quarter bin.
Richest is not what Gideon says. His words are, “my clan is the weakest in Manasseh” (Judges 6:15). He's making the case that he's a bad pick for the job.
A big clan would have made his case harder to argue. Gideon says the opposite: “my clan is the weakest in Manasseh” (Judges 6:15). That's the whole point of his answer.
It's the reverse. Gideon says, “I am the youngest in my father's house” (Judges 6:15). So he's the youngest, not the oldest. He's laying out every reason he can think of.
Right. Gideon says, “I am the youngest in my father's house” (Judges 6:15). He says it right after calling his clan the weakest in Manasseh. He's stacking up his reasons like dough bowls.

Gideon says, “give me a sign that it is You speaking with me” (Judges 6:17). He wants something he can see. And notice the LORD doesn't turn him away, since the offering that follows is how the sign comes.
No scroll in this verse. Gideon asks, “give me a sign that it is You speaking with me” (Judges 6:17). He's asking for something he can see, not something he can read.
Gideon doesn't go looking for a witness. He says, “give me a sign that it is You speaking with me” (Judges 6:17). A sign is something he can see for himself.

explanations.answer: A young goat and unleavened bread
explanations.explanation: Judges 6:19 says Gideon “prepared a young goat and unleavened bread and an ephah of flour.” He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot. That's real cooking, friend, and I respect the work.

explanations.answer: A lamb and a jar of honey
explanations.explanation: Lamb and honey sound like a lovely spread, but they're not on this list. Judges 6:19 says Gideon “prepared a young goat and unleavened bread and an ephah of flour.” The meat goes in a basket and the broth in a pot.

explanations.answer: A dove and a jar of oil
explanations.explanation: That's a different offering than the one Gideon makes. Judges 6:19 says he “prepared a young goat and unleavened bread and an ephah of flour.” No dove, no oil.

explanations.answer: Fire flares up from the rock
explanations.explanation: Judges 6:21 says, “fire flared from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread.” The angel only touched them with the tip of his staff. Gideon asked for a sign, and that's one you can't miss.

explanations.answer: Water pours out of the rock
explanations.explanation: Water from a rock does happen in the Bible, but not here. In this verse, “fire flared from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread” (Judges 6:21). This rock is a flame rock today.

explanations.answer: The rock splits right in two
explanations.explanation: The rock stays in one piece. What happens is that “fire flared from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread” (Judges 6:21). The staff only touches the offering, and the fire does the rest.

He doesn't stay. Judges 6:21 says, “the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.” One moment he's standing there with a staff, and the next he's gone. Gideon is left looking at a rock still glowing.
Right. After the fire, “the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight” (Judges 6:21). He was there one moment and gone the next. That's when Gideon realizes who he's been talking to.

explanations.answer: He saw the angel face to face
explanations.explanation: Gideon says, “Oh no, Lord GOD! I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!” (Judges 6:22). He only realizes who it was after the angel vanishes. The text gives us his words, and they sound like a man who just got a big surprise.

explanations.answer: He made the angel wait too long
explanations.explanation: Gideon did ask the angel to wait while he got his offering, and the LORD said, “I will stay until you return” (Judges 6:18). But that's not what he cries out about. He says, “I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!” (Judges 6:22).

explanations.answer: He gave the angel too little
explanations.explanation: The offering isn't what Gideon is upset about. His words are, “Oh no, Lord GOD! I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!” (Judges 6:22). The text says nothing about the gift being too small.
He does. The LORD says, “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die” (Judges 6:23). Gideon had just cried out in alarm, and these are the words that answer him. Short, calm and clear.

It's true, because the LORD says it out loud. His words are, “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die” (Judges 6:23). Gideon had just said he'd seen the angel of the LORD face to face, and this is the answer he gets.
Gideon “called it The LORD Is Peace” (Judges 6:24). It comes right after the LORD told him, “Peace be with you.” And the text says the altar still stood in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

That's a real name from the Bible, but it belongs somewhere else. Abraham, the father of Israel's people, named a place “The LORD Will Provide” (Genesis 22:14). Gideon's altar is called “The LORD Is Peace” (Judges 6:24).
That's the name of a different altar. Moses, Israel's leader, built one and called it “The LORD Is My Banner” (Exodus 17:15). Gideon names his altar “The LORD Is Peace” (Judges 6:24).
The LORD says, “tear down your father's altar to Baal” (Judges 6:25). Gideon's own father has an altar to Baal, a false god, right there at home. So the job starts in his own family's backyard.

You might expect the first job to be against Midian, but not yet. The LORD says, “tear down your father's altar to Baal, and cut down the Asherah pole beside it” (Judges 6:25). This first task is much closer to home.
The oak is where Gideon met the angel (Judges 6:11), and it stays right where it is. What the LORD tells him to tear down is “your father's altar to Baal” (Judges 6:25). The tree isn't on the list.

explanations.answer: A proper altar to the LORD
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “build a proper altar to the LORD your God on the top of this stronghold” (Judges 6:26). Out goes the altar to Baal, and up goes an altar to the LORD. The Asherah pole's wood gets used for the burnt offering, so nothing goes to waste.

A watchtower sounds sensible with Midian around, but it's not the order. The LORD tells him, “build a proper altar to the LORD your God on the top of this stronghold” (Judges 6:26). The building project is for worship.

Shelters were what the Israelites were building when Midian was around (Judges 6:2). But that's not what the LORD asks here. He says, “build a proper altar to the LORD your God on the top of this stronghold” (Judges 6:26).
Daylight is not how it went. Judges 6:27 says Gideon “did it by night rather than in the daytime.” He took ten servants along, so it wasn't a one-man job.
Right. Judges 6:27 says he “did it by night rather than in the daytime.” With ten servants and a whole altar to tear down, that's a big night's work.

explanations.answer: He fears his father's household and the city
explanations.explanation: Judges 6:27 says he was “too afraid of his father's household and the men of the city,” so he did it by night. The text gives us that reason plainly. He still did what the LORD told him, afraid and all.

explanations.answer: The LORD told him to keep it all a secret
explanations.explanation: The LORD gives the orders about the altar and the pole, but the text never says to keep it secret. The reason it gives is that Gideon was “too afraid of his father's household and the men of the city” (Judges 6:27).

explanations.answer: His servants could only work after dark
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says that about the servants. Judges 6:27 says Gideon took ten of them, and that he did it by night because he was “too afraid of his father's household and the men of the city.”

They do. Judges 6:28 says, “there was Baal's altar torn down, with the Asherah pole cut down beside it and the second bull offered up on the newly built altar.” Imagine waking up to that view. No one in that city had a quiet morning.

It's true, because the whole scene is waiting for them. Judges 6:28 says, “there was Baal's altar torn down, with the Asherah pole cut down beside it and the second bull offered up on the newly built altar.” Everything the LORD told Gideon to do had been done.

They say, “Bring out your son. He must die” (Judges 6:30). They give a reason too: he tore down Baal's altar and cut down the Asherah pole. This is a heavy moment for Gideon, and I think it's good to say so plainly.
They don't stop at sending him away. The men of the city tell Joash, “Bring out your son. He must die” (Judges 6:30). It's a serious moment, so I'll just say it straight.

They aren't asking for payment. The text says they told Joash, “Bring out your son. He must die, because he has torn down Baal's altar and cut down the Asherah pole beside it” (Judges 6:30). That's a heavy thing to say about a son.

Joash goes the other way. He tells the crowd, “If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the one who has torn down his altar” (Judges 6:31). He stands up to the men instead of handing his son over.

Right. Joash says to all who stood against him, “If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the one who has torn down his altar” (Judges 6:31). He doesn't hand Gideon over. The crowd came for his son and left without him.

Joash says, “If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the one who has torn down his altar” (Judges 6:31). Baal's the one with the broken altar, so let him do the talking. It's a sharp answer from a man with a whole crowd in front of him.

Fire from heaven isn't in Joash's words. He tells the crowd, “If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the one who has torn down his altar” (Judges 6:31). The challenge is for Baal to speak up for himself.

Joash doesn't tell Baal to rebuild anything. His words are, “If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the one who has torn down his altar” (Judges 6:31). He wants Baal to take his own case up with Gideon.

Judges 6:32 says Gideon was called Jerubbaal, “that is to say, ‘Let Baal contend with him,’ because he had torn down Baal's altar.” The man who was hiding wheat now has a brand new name. And it picks up Joash's own challenge.
That's what the angel told Gideon at the winepress: “The LORD is with you” (Judges 6:12). But it's not what Jerubbaal means. The verse says it means “Let Baal contend with him” (Judges 6:32).
The altar did fall, but that's not what the name says. Judges 6:32 gives the meaning: “Let Baal contend with him.” It's a challenge, not a report.
